Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is among the most lethal solid tumors [@siegel2026cancer]. Its clinical heterogeneity reflects variation in both malignant cells and the surrounding microenvironment. Bulk transcriptomic studies have identified clinically relevant malignant and stromal states in PDAC: basal-like and classical tumor programs [@collisson2011subtypes; @moffitt2015virtual; @rashid2020purity], and, from single-cell-informed analyses, tumor-promoting proCAF and tumor-restraining restCAF stromal programs [@peng2024determination]. Single-cell and spatial profiling have further shown that this heterogeneity extends across malignant, stromal, immune, and other microenvironmental compartments within individual tumors [@moncada2020spatial; @hwang2022single; @werba2023single]. Expression-defined programs can be evaluated against survival after discovery [@collisson2011subtypes; @Bailey2016]. Whether allowing survival to shape program definitions can identify a tumor--stroma program that provides prognostic information beyond established classifications remains unclear. Such programs could provide candidates for prognostic assays and trial stratification, while identifying genes and biological processes for further investigation.

Addressing this question requires large cohorts with survival-annotated transcriptomic data, which in PDAC are still derived primarily from bulk profiling [@aung2018compass]. Bulk profiles, however, mix signals from malignant and microenvironmental cells [@nguyen2024fourteen]. Nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) and related deconvolution methods separate these composite profiles into interpretable gene programs, defined as weighted sets of co-varying genes that together form a representation of the tumor transcriptome [@lee1999learning; @brunet2004metagenes; @moffitt2015virtual; @peng2019novo]. In PDAC, these approaches have supported molecular subtype discovery and subsequent single-sample classification [@collisson2011subtypes; @Bailey2016; @rashid2020purity], virtual microdissection of tumor- and stroma-specific expression [@moffitt2015virtual], and compartment-specific tumor--stroma characterization [@peng2019novo; @peng2024determination]. When predefined signatures are applied unchanged to a bulk cohort, survival can be used to assess their prognostic relevance but does not alter their gene definitions during that application. The challenge is therefore to let survival shape the programs as they are learned, to retain a decomposed representation rather than only a risk score, and to test those same programs, unchanged, across independent studies.

Standard NMF learns gene programs by minimizing reconstruction error, the mismatch between the measured expression matrix and its approximation rebuilt from the programs. Such reconstruction-driven criteria favor patterns that capture prominent expression variation regardless of their relevance to patient survival [@bair2004semi; @cook2007fisher]. This is particularly important in PDAC, where bulk tumors contain substantial stromal, exocrine, and other non-malignant signals that can dominate transcriptomic variation and obscure less prominent but prognostically relevant programs [@rashid2020purity; @torrehealy2023pdacr; @peng2024determination; @aran2015systematic].

Reconstruction alone also does not uniquely identify the gene programs without additional constraints [@donoho2004nmf; @laurberg2008uniqueness; @gillis2014nmf], which may contribute to cross-study variability among proposed unsupervised PDAC subtype taxonomies [@lautizi2022pancreatic]. The basal-like/classical dichotomy developed over roughly a decade of iterative subtyping, virtual microdissection, independent cohorts, single-cell analyses and prospective clinical profiling [@collisson2011subtypes; @moffitt2015virtual; @rashid2020purity; @werba2023single; @aung2018compass], and comparable work on stromal CAF subtypes is under way [@peng2024determination]. Survival information offers an additional criterion for shaping discovery, although it does not by itself resolve this non-uniqueness.

Survival-supervised models such as penalized Cox regression and supervised principal components identify outcome-associated expression patterns, but do not explicitly separate those patterns into malignant and microenvironmental programs [@bair2004semi; @simon2011regularization]. PDAC subtypes and their single-sample classifiers, however, are defined at the program level [@rashid2020purity; @peng2024determination].

Here, we present DeSurv, a survival-supervised matrix factorization framework that integrates NMF with Cox regression, moving clinical relevance from a post hoc criterion to one that shapes gene programs during discovery. Because the factorization is sensitive to initialization, solutions from many independent restarts are aggregated to initialize a final fit. The resulting gene weights are then held fixed, or frozen, so the same learned programs can be tested in external cohorts without refitting the representation.

We evaluate DeSurv in PDAC by comparing the resulting representation with unsupervised NMF at matched and higher rank (the number of programs the factorization extracts) and with conventional survival models such as penalized Cox regression and supervised principal components (Supplementary Table \ref{tab:architecture}). We then evaluate the clinical relevance of the frozen programs in independent cohorts and ask whether they retain prognostic information beyond established PDAC classifiers. Simulations in which the true underlying (latent) programs are known characterize the conditions under which survival supervision improves recovery of prognostic structure.
